project: FL-IDS: Making Federated Learning More Secure and More Private
description: Network-layer intrusion detection model (Model 1 of the dual-model FL-IDS architecture). Detects volumetric and protocol-level attacks via packet/flow features. This baseline uses NO Byzantine attack, NO defenses (Krum/DP/HE/ZKP all disabled), NO learning-rate decay, and NO EMA smoothing — plain FedProx only.

correctness_prerequisites.description: This run is only valid because of two prior bug fixes to the data pipeline. Both are documented here so this manifest is self-contained.

label_mapping_bug.found_via: verify_label_bug.py, cross-checked against raw CSV value_counts()
label_mapping_bug.root_cause: sklearn.LabelEncoder.fit() sorts classes ALPHABETICALLY regardless of input list order. The original code assumed ALL_CLASSES list order (0=Normal, 7=DDoS_TCP, etc.) matched the encoder's assigned indices. It did not: alphabetically, index 7 was actually 'Normal', not 'DDoS_TCP'.
label_mapping_bug.consequence: 14 of 15 classes were mislabeled. The 'DDoS_TCP cap to 18%' step was actually capping Normal (which really is 72.8% of the raw data) while true DDoS_TCP (2.26% of data) passed through uncapped. NETWORK_ORIG_IDX and APP_ORIG_IDX selected the wrong 8-class subsets for both models.
label_mapping_bug.fix: Replaced LabelEncoder with an explicit dict comprehension: {name: i for i, name in enumerate(ALL_CLASSES)}, guaranteeing ALL_CLASSES[i] and y==i always agree.
label_mapping_bug.verified_by: verify_data_loader.py, run against a stratified sample covering all 15 real classes — all label_mapping and cap-target checks PASS.

majority_class_cap_correction.old_belief: DDoS_TCP represents 72.8% of the dataset (a lab artefact) and must be capped to 18% (VARS-FL methodology).
majority_class_cap_correction.corrected_finding: Normal is the true 72.8% majority class. DDoS_TCP is genuinely only ~2.26% of the raw data and does not need capping. The cap target was changed from 'DDoS_TCP' to 'Normal' to match reality, preserving the original 18% VARS-FL ratio methodology.
majority_class_cap_correction.verification: Post-fix rebuild produced 736,046 total rows with Normal at exactly 18.00% — matches the VARS-FL paper's target ratio and is a strong independent sanity check that the fix is correct.

dataset.source: Edge-IIoTset DNN subset (DNN-EdgeIIoT-dataset.csv, ~1.2GB, 2,219,201 raw rows, 63 raw columns)
dataset.cap_methodology: VARS-FL (arXiv 2605.05896, Section IV-A): cap the true majority class (Normal) to 18% of the post-cap total.

class_definition.note: MITM (1,214) and Ransomware (10,925) are the smallest classes and show the weakest/most volatile performance in results below — consistent with limited sample availability, not necessarily a fixable modeling issue.

preprocessing.feature_selection_method: VarianceThreshold(threshold=1e-6) applied to remove near-zero-variance columns
preprocessing.scaling: StandardScaler (zero mean, unit variance), fit after VarianceThreshold and after class capping
preprocessing.text_columns: NOT engineered for this model (tcp.payload, http.request.full_uri, etc. are dropped/zeroed via VarianceThreshold — the network model relies on raw packet/flow-level numeric features only, unlike the application model)
preprocessing.historical_bug_fixed: Original VarianceThreshold(1e-6) run before StandardScaler caused near-zero-variance columns (e.g. udp.port) to produce NaN under StandardScaler, silently zeroing the only features distinguishing DDoS_UDP from DDoS_TCP. Fixed by ensuring VarianceThreshold always precedes StandardScaler in the pipeline order.

layers: Conv1d(1, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1) -> GroupNorm(8,64) or BatchNorm1d(64) -> ReLU -> MaxPool1d(2)
Conv1d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1) -> GroupNorm(8,128) or BatchNorm1d(128) -> ReLU -> MaxPool1d(2)
LSTM(input=128 [computed via dummy forward pass], hidden=64, num_layers=1, batch_first=True) or DPLSTM if dp_safe
model_architecture.note_on_dp_safe: dp_safe=False uses standard BatchNorm1d + nn.LSTM (this run). dp_safe=True (GroupNorm + DPLSTM) is required only when USE_DP=True (Opacus DP-SGD), not used in this baseline.

loss_function.class_weighting: inverse-sqrt of live class counts (get_class_counts_network()), NOT clamped in this run
loss_function.clamping_status: UNCLAMPED — this baseline predates the two-sided weight clamp fix (_clamp_class_weights, min_mult=0.3, max_mult=2.5). Computed unclamped weights: MITM ~3.8x mean, Ransomware ~1.3x mean, all other classes 0.37-0.59x mean. This is documented as a KNOWN LIMITATION of this specific baseline — see 'known_limitations' below.
loss_function.manual_overrides: none (manual per-class weight overrides were only ever applied to the application model, not network)

federated_learning_config.learning_rate_schedule: NONE — static learning rate across all 25 rounds (LR decay feature exists in main.py but was NOT used for this run per explicit configuration choice)
federated_learning_config.optimizer: Adam, recreated fresh every client every round
federated_learning_config.within_round_lr_schedule: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(step_size=3, gamma=0.95) — applied WITHIN each round's 5 local epochs only, resets every round
federated_learning_config.aggregation: FedProx (weighted FedAvg with proximal term in client loss)
federated_learning_config.partitioning: Dirichlet non-IID, alpha=0.7, seed=42, across 10 clients. Classes with <2 samples per client dropped from that client's partition (real non-IID behavior).
federated_learning_config.ema_smoothing: DISABLED for this run (EMA feature exists in main.py, decay=0.9, but was not used per explicit configuration choice)
federated_learning_config.parallelization: 4-worker persistent ProcessPoolExecutor, 3 threads/worker (12 cores detected). Per-client training parallelized; ZKP/HE/Krum bookkeeping and evaluation remain sequential in original client order.

defenses_and_attacks.note: This is a clean baseline run — no privacy or robustness mechanisms active. Establishes the reference point against which Experiment 1 (Krum+DP interaction), Experiment 2 (HE blind spot), and Experiment 3 (combined privacy stack) will be compared.

metric_definitions.f1_macro: unweighted mean of per-class F1 across all 8 classes
metric_definitions.round_time_s: wall-clock seconds for one full FL round (parallel client training + aggregation + evaluation)

best_round.selection_criterion: best accuracy AND best F1-Macro simultaneously across all 25 rounds
best_round.IMPORTANT_CAVEAT: This round's actual trained model weights are NOT recoverable from disk. checkpoint_network.npz only ever holds the LAST round's weights (round 25 in this run, which was a degraded round), because best-checkpoint saving was not enabled for this run. Round 22 is documented here as the best NUMBER achieved, not as a currently-loadable model. To make this round's weights reproducible, either re-enable best-checkpoint saving in main.py, or accept that only round 25's weights are on disk.

round_25_anomaly.description: Round 25 shows a sharp, unexplained regression: Accuracy 0.9549 (round 24) -> 0.8090, F1-Macro 0.8217 -> 0.6800. Ransomware collapses 0.7929 -> 0.2773, DDoS_HTTP collapses 0.7531 -> 0.4409, while the three largest classes (DDoS_UDP, DDoS_ICMP, DDoS_TCP) barely move.

confusion_matrix_diagnosis.evaluated_on: checkpoint_network.npz — i.e. round 25's model specifically (the only round available, since best-checkpoint saving was not enabled)
confusion_matrix_diagnosis.finding: Ransomware acted as a false-positive 'attractor' class: its own recall was 100%, but multiple OTHER true classes were misclassified INTO Ransomware at high rates.

misclassification_into_ransomware.Normal: 16.9% of true Normal predicted as Ransomware
misclassification_into_ransomware.DDoS_HTTP: 28.5% of true DDoS_HTTP predicted as Ransomware (only 32.2% correct)
misclassification_into_ransomware.Vulnerability_scanner: 39.0% of true Vulnerability_scanner predicted as Ransomware (only 51.2% correct)
misclassification_into_ransomware.MITM: 69.0% of true MITM predicted as Ransomware (only 31.0% correct)

confusion_matrix_diagnosis.likely_mechanism: Ransomware's class weight was unclamped (~1.3x mean) and MITM's was ~3.8x mean with no ceiling (see loss_function.clamping_status above). An over-weighted class's misclassifications cost the loss function more, pushing the decision boundary to favor false positives for that class. A two-sided weight clamp fix (min_mult=0.3, max_mult=2.5) exists in a later revision of task.py but was NOT active for this baseline run.

known_limitations: Class weights are UNCLAMPED on the high end for this run — MITM gets an unbounded ~3.8x weight boost, Ransomware ~1.3x, contributing to the round-25 Ransomware-attractor collapse documented above.

MITM (1,214 real samples) plateaus around F1=0.41-0.48 for nearly the entire run and never breaks past 0.50 even at the best round (0.4514) — consistent with genuine sample scarcity under Dirichlet(alpha=0.7) partitioning across 10 clients, not necessarily a fixable weighting/architecture issue.

Round-to-round F1-Macro variance is substantial (e.g. round 9 dips to 0.6940 after round 8's 0.7571; round 25 crashes to 0.6800 from round 24's 0.8217) — no LR decay or EMA smoothing is active in this baseline, so this variance is NOT damped.
The 'best round' (22) is a NUMBER only — its actual model weights were overwritten by rounds 23-25 before being saved separately, because best-checkpoint tracking was not enabled for this run.

The confusion-matrix diagnosis above reflects round 25 (the worst round of the run) because that is the only checkpoint that exists on disk — it is NOT representative of the best-round (22) model's confusion pattern, which has never been directly measured.

PROX_MU=0.02 was chosen empirically after observing that PROX_MU=0.1 converged too slowly (still climbing at round 25 in an earlier application-model test) and PROX_MU=0.01 produced severe round-to-round oscillation. 0.02 was not exhaustively tuned against the network model specifically — it was carried over from application-model experimentation.

No cross-validation or held-out final test set beyond the standard 80/20 per-client split under Dirichlet partitioning — reported F1/accuracy are on each client's local 20% test split, aggregated by simple mean across 10 clients, which can be noisy for classes concentrated on few clients (e.g. MITM, Ransomware).

reproducibility.framework: custom Python simulation (direct, parallel client training via ProcessPoolExecutor)
reproducibility.experiment_config_json: experiment_config_network.json (auto-generated by main.py at run start, contains the exact runtime flag values)
